subject: gramophone
pitch: An antique gramophone on a carved walnut cabinet. A huge flaring brass horn shaped like a morning-glory flower, a black record with a red label on the turntable, a silver tonearm, a wind-up crank on the side and little claw feet. The brass has a warm, slightly green patina, and the wood is inlaid with a pale floral pattern.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the gramophone module structure, noting that I'll need a root joint since part() requires one to resolve against, plus likely additional joints for the crank, tonearm, and turntable components.

For dimensions, I'm sketching out a cabinet roughly 0.42m square with 0.30m height sitting on 0.05m feet, with the brass horn emerging from the back-top and curving upward and forward like a swan-neck toward a flared bell opening. I'm working out the sweep path with curved points from the horn's base near the cabinet up through several control points to the bell, planning an exponential radius expansion for the morning-glory flare and considering a patina paint treatment mixing brass and teal-green tones for an aged look.

I want the horn to appear hollow with a darker interior lining near the opening, so I'm working out how to add a dark disc cap positioned slightly inward from the bell's end, computing the end frame orientation from the path's tangent to place the disc correctly facing outward with a slightly reduced radius to suggest depth.

Now I'm adding a torus rim around the bell opening oriented along the tangent direction, then moving on to the horn's base mounting into a brass elbow on the cabinet, and starting to build the cabinet body as a box geometry.

For the cabinet, I'm adding feet, a top lid plate, and a plinth base moulding, plus claw feet at the corners made from spheres and toe sweeps with tapered leg rods. For the finish, I'm applying walnut grain texture to the wood and planning a floral inlay decal on the front panel.

Now I'm placing the decal on the front face with a cream floral SVG pattern of petals, leaves, and vines over a transparent background, mirrored onto the sides, and adding corner pilasters in lighter wood plus crown moulding and a raised inset panel on the front.

For the top of the cabinet, I'm working out the turntable platter dimensions and placement relative to the lid height and the horn's position, making sure the green felt platter cylinder fits within the lid's z-extents without colliding with the horn base.

Now I'm designing the record itself with a black cylinder shaped using radial distance from its axis to paint subtle concentric groove bands, then adding a red label disc with a gold ring accent and a brass spindle cylinder at the center.

I'm setting these record parts to attach under a "turntable" joint positioned above the lid, then working out the tonearm — a brass pivot post on the right-back side with a joint for the arm that sweeps from the pivot toward the record.

The arm follows a curved silver path to a head shell with a needle positioned to rest within the record's radius, plus a counterweight sphere at the back, all parented to the tonearm bone so it can pivot. Now I'm moving on to designing the crank mechanism.

I don't think extra joints are needed for feet or a crank arm role, so I'll skip those. For the horn, I'm placing the starting point near the lid interior and adding a brass collar with a lathed profile that flares out before tapering back to the axis, keeping the loop closed automatically.

Now I'm shaping the horn's flare using a radius function that grows cubically with a slight linear boost, mimicking a morning-glory bell that widens sharply near the end, reaching about 0.33 at the tip. I'm positioning the bell's end center above the lid and checking that the tangent direction from the last curve points mostly forward so the bell doesn't dip below the lid surface.

I tweak the ending tangent to angle more steeply upward—around 34°—and recompute the lowest point of the bell, confirming it clears the turntable's lid height. The bell's width ends up roughly 0.66 across, much wider than the cabinet itself, which matches the exaggerated horn look I want, and total height comes out around 1 unit.

Now I'm thinking through surface treatment for the horn: a mottled brass-and-teal patina paint for weathering, a brighter brass for the rim torus, and considering adding fluted ridges along the horn's length using a striped paint pattern based on angular coordinates to simulate 16 decorative flutes.

Working out the disc placement inside the bell—orienting it to face outward along the tangent direction so it's visible when looking into the bell opening, and calculating the position and radius near the end of the sweep.

Now I'm designing the feet for the piece: brass or dark wood ball feet at the corners with small claw-toe spikes radiating outward and tilted downward, plus a connecting leg block joining each foot up to the body.

Now I'm laying out the cabinet structure: plinth box, main body, and lid stacked with specific y-ranges, then positioning the front decal panel centered on the body face.

For the side panels, I'm computing their decal direction and size, then working through crank placement so it doesn't collide with the floral decal region—settling on an upper position offset in z and y to keep it clear.

I'm also sketching small decorative details: corner pilasters as darker wood boxes, skipping the brake lever and tonearm rest as unnecessary, and planning an SVG floral pattern with a central five-petal flower, smaller side flowers, and leaves in a pale cream palette.

Now I'm structuring the code: defining the turntable part with explicit bone weighting, using the root joint by default, building sweep paths from Catmull-Rom curves and polylines for the crank, and applying filleted skinning for smooth rounded corners.

Adding platter cylinder and spindle geometry...

Setting up the tonearm joint and base post, headshell box, and needle cone...

Working out the needle tip position and counterweight sphere placement behind the pivot...

Now I'm writing the part-building helper for boxes with consistent wood grain paint, double-checking I stay under the 64-color limit, and deciding to skip the horn support brace to keep things simple.
